posts.post_subject: Panchromatic silver halide on the cheap w/dyes?
posts.content_md:
Hi all!

I'm strongly considering getting into some color holography but am appalled at the price of panchromatic emulsions. What's available commercially is not only ridiculously expensive but also seems to only come in strange sizes. I need an alternative.

By now I've basically learned how to reliably get holograms on VRP-M. VRP-M claims to be sensitive to 488-530nm. I've been lasing at 532nm and will likely be adding one of Dave B's 488nm lasers to my setup, along with a red laser of currently unknown wavelength.

By my reckoning, VRP-M should already be thirsty for the blue and green I'll be using, and I'm wondering if it will be possible to just add some dye (green dye? blue dye?) to the emulsion before exposure and get it to also be red-sensitive.

I'm certain I'm over-simplifying this, and answers will likely involve heavy-duty chemistry and molecular binding or other stuff I feel dumb just thinking about. Please, guys, bear in mind that I could probably be legally declared a moron, so if you don't mind - maybe keep the answers kinda short-bus for me?

Infinite thanks, guys!

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Panchromatic silver halide on the cheap w/dyes?
posts.content_md:
> **holorefugee:** What problems are you having?

Well, the film is very, very soft. So, after I shoot it, I can't dry it with a hair dryer, it takes forever and finally the film crazes. If I leave it to dry on it's own overnight, there's nothing there the next day. Sometimes the film has come right off the glass. I tried pre-hardening with formaldehyde and again, no results. The film does dry under the hair dryer, but I get no image. The exposure figures given on Slavich site don't seem to work. I've heard that the red is insensitive, so I've given it milliwatts (as if it were resist or dcg) and still nothing.

I think that my problem is getting the right exposure/pre-hardening timings and concentrations (for the pre-hardeing mixture) Unfortunately, it's expensive enough that I can't go through a box of film just to get the right exposure with the right amount of pre-hardening. I can get green, but I don't know of anyone who's made colour in 03C and is willing to talk!

> **Justin W:** Which would be easier, sensitizing red film for blue and green or sensitizing green film for red and blue?

Dam good question! My feeling is sensitizing red film for green/blue. The reason is that the spatial frequencies are higher for green/blue so the fringes are closer together. Thus, the dye energy transfer is localised.

posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** holorefugee wrote:What problems are you having?Well, the film is very, very soft. So, after I shoot it, I can't dry it with a hair dryer, it takes forever and finally the film crazes. If I leave it to dry on it's own overnight, there's nothing there the next day. Sometimes the film has come right off the glass. I tried pre-hardening with formaldehyde and again, no results. The film does dry under the hair dryer, but I get no image. The exposure figures given on Slavich site don't seem to work. I've heard that the red is insensitive, so I've given it milliwatts (as if it were resist or dcg) and still nothing.I think that my problem is getting the right exposure/pre-hardening timings and concentrations (for the pre-hardeing mixture) Unfortunately, it's expensive enough that I can't go through a box of film just to get the right exposure with the right amount of pre-hardening. I can get green, but I don't know of anyone who's made colour in 03C and is willing to talk!.

I've gotten some good results with PFG-3c, and its definitely a pain.

For drying, hurrying it up works poorly... I've used a small fan (like a computer fan) blowing on the plate leaning nearly vertical on something. Just air-drying it takes an hour or two, with the fan maybe 1/2 hour. 

For exposure, the datasheet says 3.5 milijoules/cm^2, and I've gotten good results there (with 532nm). I don't entirely trust my meter's calibration though. The film seems to come from the factory pre-fogged. I've gotten my best results using Jeff's anti-fog bath. Which means drying the plates twice... So my routine is usually anti-fog the plates one day, let them dry overnight, and then holograms the next day (or next weekend). At 8 millijoules/cm^2, the results were brighter, but my setup wasn't stable enough, so it was just a band of brightness in one corner of the plate.

For the rest of the chemistry, I used JD-4 developer (30 seconds), ferric EDTA bleach (till-clear and then 30 seconds more, typically 1:45 or so), then 15 seconds in a 2.5 percent solution of potassium dichromate to kill the dyes, and finally a rinse in photo-flo (but not enough to wash out all the dichromate in hopes of avoiding print-out).

posts.content_md:
> **Martin:** Have you ever tried to dry the emulsion à la DCG, that's to say, dehydrating it in an alcohol bath?

No, actually, and it's interesting you say that. I used to dry the old Agfa plates in alcohol because that's the way I was taught to do it with Edwina and Peter Miller. When I transferred to Kodak for the brief period between the end of Agfa and the beginning of Slavich, I continued to dry in alcohol. However,, when I dried Slavich in alcohol the image disappeared! I finally found one of Hans Bjelkhagen's papers stating that Slavich will lose the image when dried with alcohol, so I stopped the practice. It never occurred to me to go back to drying in alcohol.

> **Martin:** Sounds like the emulsion lost its red sensivity

Possible, or it's a stability issue. The setup was designed for an exposure of less than a minute and I was shooting for over 5 minutes sometimes.

> **Tommy:** The film seems to come from the factory pre-fogged.

I've found that the film goes instantly black in the developer (CWC2) and I assumed that the film was fogged. However, all batches of the film over a period of several months all exhibited the same behaviour. If the odd batch was fogged, I can understand that soemone was sloppy and exposed the film to white light, but *all* batches over several months? I find that hard to accept. But, it's the results I have. I see a disgruntled employee at Slavich grasping the lid of the 03C box and saying, "They want colour? I'll give 'em colour!" and opening the box lid. Joking, just joking!

But, when I reduce the exposure to low levels and use a dim orange led as a safelight, it doesn't go dark instantly. However, the low exposure seems to be too low, leading again to a chicken-and-egg situation. I have talked to Bob Hess about this and he told me that you need to ignore the instant darkening and just keep going with the developement. Of course, it's impossible to determine the development time by density so I tried this and simply developed to two minutes. Result? Nothing!

> **Tommy:** For exposure, the datasheet says 3.5 milijoules/cm^2, and I've gotten good results there (with 532nm).

Have you tried all three colours? I can get individual green and even red, but when I try all three, I lose all image. I know it can be done because apparently Rabbitholes uses 03C, but there seems to be some vital part of the (pre) processing technique that I'm missing. 

However, I hope to try the anti-fogging technique as well as Colin's suggestion of post-hardening with formaldehyde. Hopefully post results soon.
